Obedience

/oh-BEE-dee-uhns/ - the stress falls on BEE · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Obedience means the practice of doing what one is told.

Basic training drills obedience into recruits long before anyone trusts them with a decision of their own.

Worked Example

The fire academy's first month is pure obedience: when the captain says out, you go out, even if you cannot see why. On Ruiz's third live burn, the order came mid-sweep — out, now — and he obeyed with the nozzle still charged. Moments later the ceiling he had been standing under let go.

Obedience is the exact word for what saved him, because obedience means the practice of doing what one is told — practiced until it outruns argument. Trust is underneath it, but trust is a feeling; obedience is the doing, order by order, whether or not the reasons arrive in time.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dutifulness: Dutifulness is doing what duty requires, orders or none — the dutiful nurse double-checks the chart because the role demands it, not because anyone said so. Obedience needs a voice: it is the practice of doing what one is told, order by order, by someone with standing to tell.

discipline: Discipline is order kept from inside yourself — your own rules and standards, followed when nobody is watching. Obedience answers to someone else: the order arrives from outside and is carried out. A student keeping her own training log shows discipline; running laps because the coach said so is obedience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

defiance: refusing an order to its face

insubordination: the soldier's word for refusing a superior

Where it sits · how fully one's own judgment is surrendered — cooperation → obedience → subservience

cooperation vs. obedience: Cooperation is milder than obedience — cooperating teammates trade suggestions and split decisions with nobody in command, while obedience hands each decision to whoever gives the order.

subservience vs. obedience: Subservience goes further than obedience — the obedient crew carries out the order it is given, while subservience moves before the order comes and surrenders judgment entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ob-

Prefix — ob-: toward (Latin)

Root — edi

Root — edi: to hear (Latin audire, worn down inside the word)

Suffix — -ence

Suffix — -ence: noun ending: the practice of

Put it together

Put it together: Ob- (toward) + edi (to hear — audire, worn smooth inside the word) + -ence = the practice of listening toward someone. Latin oboedire built obeying out of hearing: to obey is to keep an ear turned to the one giving orders, and obedience is that listening made into habit.

Use the root in a new word: audience

Use the root in a new word: audience: An audience is literally 'the hearers' — the same audire root, seated in rows and doing nothing but listening.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / disciplined

Obedience is doing as told — a relationship to commands and the people giving them. Compliant, its unit-mate, answers written rules rather than voices; docile names the temperament that makes obeying easy; servile is obedience spoiled, eager past the point of dignity. Obedience itself takes no sides: on a rope team or a flight deck it can be the safest thing there is.
